personalize.e: Middle English personal English personal Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English personalize From personal + -ize.

d.g: To fraudulently portray another person; to impersonate.
d.x: But this latter has, at the suggestion of Tyndarus, exchanged clothes with him, and the slave[…] personates the master.

d.g: To portray a character (as in a play); to act.
To attribute personal characteristics to something; to personify.
d.x: One do I personate of Timon's frame , Whom Fortune with her iv'ry hand wafts to her

d.g: To set forth in an unreal character; to disguise; to mask.
d.x: a personated mate

d.g: To be an example of; to have all the attributes of.
d.x: Mozart could be said to personify musical genius.

d.g: To create a representation of (an abstract quality) in the form of a character or persona.
d.x: The writer personified death in the form of the Grim Reaper.

personify.e: From French personnifier. By surface analysis, person + -ify or person(a) + -ify.

d.g: To emit (sweat or perspiration) through the skin's pores.
d.x: I was perspiring freely after running the marathon.

d.g: To be evacuated or excreted, or to exude, through the pores of the skin.
d.x: A fluid perspires.

d.g: To cause (someone) to sweat.
d.x: Outside his window a long, humid summer, the first hot season of the third millennium, baked and perspired.

perspire.e: Borrowed from Middle French perspirer and its source Latin perspīrō (“to breathe everywhere, blow constantly”), from per (“through”) + spīrō (“to breathe”); see spirit.

d.g: To successfully convince (someone) to agree to, accept, or do something, usually through reasoning and verbal influence.
d.x: That salesman was able to persuade me into buying this bottle of lotion.

persuade.e: From Latin persuādeō (“to persuade”). Cognate to for, sweet.

d.g: To belong to or be connected as a part, adjunct, attribute, or accessory.
d.x: That spare wheel pertains to this car.

d.g: To relate to, concern, or be relevant to.
d.x: That question doesn't pertain to the topic, so I'm not going to answer it.

d.g: To apply; to be or remain in place; to continue to be applicable.
To be appropriate or suitable.

pertain.e: From Middle English pertenen, from Old French partenir, pertenir (modern French appartenir), in turn from Latin pertineō, pertinēre.

ori.label: Holding & grasping
ori.gloss: holding something firmly; possession and tenacity

d.g: To cause (something) to be physically disordered or disturbed; to cause confusion.
d.x: Mary therefore the more knaue art thou I ſay / That perturbeſt the worde of god I ſay […]

d.g: To disturb (someone, their mind, etc.) mentally; to bother, trouble, upset.
d.x: He remembered how, […] his childish imagination was perturbed at a phenomenon, for which he could not account.

d.g: Of a celestial body: to modify the motion or orbit of (another celestial body) by exerting a gravitational force; hence (physics), to slightly modify (the motion of an object).

To slightly modify (a set of equations or their solutions), producing deviations from a simple, easily solvable problem, in order to find an approximate solution to a problem that is more difficult to solve or otherwise unsolvable.

perturb.e: From Late Middle English perturben (“to disturb (someone) mentally, disquiet; to cause disorder to (something), confuse; to hinder (something)”), from Old French perturber, and from its etymon Latin perturbāre, the present active infinitive of perturbō (“to confuse; to alarm, disturb, trouble, perturb”), from per- (int …

d.g: To examine or consider with care.
d.x: Sitting on a low stool, a few yards from her arm-chair, I examined her figure; I perused her features.

d.g: To read completely.
d.x: This survey may be made by perusing al Books and taking notice of all Mechanicall Inventions.

d.g: To look over casually; to skim.
d.x: Haynes quickly perused the message, then took it to the captain on the bridge.

d.g: To go from place to place; to wander.
d.x: I loved to straggle off in the mornings […], just perusing around for firewood.

peruse.e: From either Medieval Latin perūtor, perūsitō (“wear out”) or Anglo-Norman peruser (“use up”), originally leading to two concurrent meanings, but only those derived from "to examine" survive today. By surface analysis, per- + use.

d.g: To be in every part of; to spread through; to permeate.
d.x: Cruel wars pervade history.

pervade.e: Latin pervādōlbor. English pervade Learned borrowing from Latin pervādō.

d.g: To evaporate through a semipermeable membrane, as a method of separating liquids.
To bother, harass, or annoy persistently.
d.x: He pestered me with questions.

d.g: A bother or nuisance.
d.x: By now I presumed I had become a real pester.

pester.e: In the senses of “overcrowd (a place)” and “impede (a person)”: from Middle French and Old French empestrer (“encumber”), influenced by English pest. The modern sense is an extension of the sense “infest”. Comparable to English construction pest + -er (used to form frequentative verbs).

d.g: To turn to stone: to harden organic matter by permeating with water and depositing dissolved minerals.
d.x: a river that petrifies any sort of wood or leaves

d.g: To produce rigidity akin to stone.
To immobilize with fright.
To become stone, or of a stony hardness, as organic matter by calcareous deposits.

petrify.e: From Middle French pétrifier, from Medieval Latin petrificāre, from Latin petra (“rock”), from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “rock”) + -ficāre, from facere (“do, make”), equivalent to petro- + -ify.

d.g: To quibble over trivial matters; nitpick.
d.x: Don't pettifog or we will soon grow weary.

d.g: To do a petty business as a lawyer, or carry out law business in a petty or tricky way.
d.x: He is a common barreter for his pleasure, that takes no money, but pettifogs gratis.
